analysis.one_liner: Ends health insurers' special exemption from federal antitrust laws against price fixing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee three weeks later, and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has exempted insurance companies from most federal antitrust laws — the laws that make price fixing illegal. This bill would strip that exemption from health insurers and medical malpractice insurers, so they could be sued and prosecuted like other companies for price fixing, bid rigging, and dividing up markets. It was introduced by Rep. John Conyers with no cosponsors and never moved past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of health insurance and medical malpractice coverage, who would gain an industry exposed to antitrust enforcement; federal antitrust enforcers, who would gain jurisdiction over health insurance markets.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the McCarran-Ferguson Act from being read to allow health insurers or medical malpractice insurers to engage in price fixing, bid rigging, or market allocation in connection with providing coverage [S2] [S3].

It amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that nothing in it modifies, impairs, or supersedes the operation of the antitrust laws with respect to the business of health insurance, and applies unfair-competition rules to health insurance regardless of whether it is carried on for profit [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and medical malpractice insurers, which would lose their antitrust exemption and face potential treble-damage lawsuits and enforcement actions for coordinated pricing.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: the McCarran-Ferguson exemption is defended as allowing insurers — especially smaller ones — to share claims data so they can price coverage accurately. Removing it could make some data-sharing arrangements legally risky and, insurers argue, push premiums up rather than down; an honest supporter would acknowledge that the premium savings, if any, are unproven.

The bill was introduced with zero cosponsors [S4], so it never had the support needed to move, and it did not include any offsetting reforms to insurance market structure that might have broadened its appeal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to consumers is real but not guaranteed: ending the exemption exposes insurers to antitrust suits for coordinated conduct, but how much that lowers premiums depends on how much such conduct actually occurs. The cost falls entirely on insurers, and the main downside for the public — possible loss of some shared-data pricing practices — is speculative. The bill's fatal weakness was political, not design: it had no cosponsors and no committee support.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee until the 113th Congress ended, with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on January 3, 2013, the first day of the 113th Congress [S1] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
On January 25, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill had no cosponsors [S4], and it received no vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health and medical malpractice insurers, which kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption and avoided any exposure to price-fixing suits. Consumers got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their antitrust exemption

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and gave introductory remarks; no one else signed on.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on January 25, 2013, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 25, 2013; the bill sat there for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: With only one sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded votes [S4] [S5], there was no visible partisan fight — the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would end their decades-long exemption from federal antitrust laws, exposing coordinated pricing to lawsuits and prosecution. Keeping the exemption shields them from the competition rules other industries face, and the cost of that shield shows up in consumers' premiums.
The bill names malpractice insurers alongside health insurers and would subject them to the same antitrust rules they are currently exempt from.
